story.title: Trump Confirms Fort Hood Shooter's Execution Will Not Be Livestreamed
story.summary: President Trump announced that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad will not be livestreamed, reversing a previous statement from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The decision follows bipartisan backlash against the Pentagon's initial plan to broadcast the execution. Families of the victims will have the option to attend the execution in person.

timeline_highlights.title: US to Livestream Execution of Fort Hood Shooter Nidal Hasan
timeline_highlights.summary: The Pentagon has announced that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed. The execution is scheduled for December 3 and will be conducted by firing squad, marking the first such military execution in the US since World War II.
key_facts: Nidal Malik Hasan was convicted for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.
The execution will be livestreamed.
It is scheduled for December 3, 2026.
This will be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II.

event_overview.title: About Military Execution
event_overview.subject: Military Execution
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the military capital case against former U.S. Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan, arising from the November 5, 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. A general court-martial sentenced Hasan to death in 2013; execution of a military death sentence is governed by the Uniform Code of Military Justice and requires completion of appellate review and presidential approval.

facts.label: Underlying attack
facts.value: On November 5, 2009, Hasan carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, Texas; official Army material states that 13 people were killed and 32 others were wounded.

facts.label: Court-martial outcome
facts.value: In August 2013, a military panel convicted Hasan of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and sentenced him to death, along with dismissal and forfeiture of pay and allowances.

facts.label: Appellate history
facts.value: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed the Army Court of Criminal Appeals’ decision in United States v. Hasan; its published digest identifies the case as 84 M.J. 181.

facts.label: Legal authority
facts.value: Under Article 57 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence may not be executed until it has been approved by the President; execution also follows completion of appellate review under service regulations.

facts.label: Administration of a military execution
facts.value: Department policy assigns each military department responsibility for policies, procedures, oversight, management, and resources for executions of service members with approved death sentences; Army materials describe the Secretary of the Army as selecting the execution date and location after presidential approval.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers October 2026 decisions and statements about carrying out this particular sentence, including public-access arrangements, rather than the full Fort Hood attack investigation, court-martial record, or all prior appeals.

explore_lenses.label: What actually changed about the execution plan?
explore_lenses.title: Broadcast canceled; execution order remains
explore_lenses.summary: The change concerns public access, not the death sentence, scheduled date, or selected method. Trump said the execution will not be streamed, while immediate victims’ families may attend in person if they choose.

claims.text: Trump said the firing-squad execution will not be livestreamed after the Pentagon had said it would be publicly streamed.
The Army’s October 7 notice set the execution for 1 p.m. CST on December 3, 2026, at Fort Hood, Texas, by firing squad; Trump’s October 15 statement did not change those elements.
Immediate family members of victims may view the execution in person, according to Trump’s statement as reported by AP and CBS.

explore_lenses.label: Why did officials object to a livestream?
explore_lenses.title: Deterrence argument met propaganda concerns
explore_lenses.summary: The documented dispute was largely over broadcasting the execution rather than over Hasan’s sentence. Supporters framed a public broadcast as deterrence; critics warned that footage could aid extremist propaganda or reduce the event to a spectacle.

claims.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said public viewing would show that there are serious consequences for such crimes; Trump likewise said a stream might have been a strong deterrent.
House Speaker Mike Johnson warned that execution video could become a recruiting tool for future terrorists.

Vice President JD Vance said Hasan should face the death penalty but said he would not watch a livestream; Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, called the proposed broadcast a promotion of a culture of death.

Officials involved in the pre-reversal discussions also worried that a video could be used in extremist propaganda and that televising the firing-squad killing of a wheelchair user would damage U.S. standing.

explore_lenses.label: What still has to happen before December 3?
explore_lenses.title: Army preparations and possible court action remain
explore_lenses.summary: The formal military approval process described by the Army has been completed through presidential approval and the setting of a date. Operational preparations and any last-minute collateral litigation could still affect whether the execution occurs on December 3.

claims.text: The Army says Trump approved Hasan’s death sentence on October 2, 2026, and Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle directed the execution on October 6 after the appellate process had upheld the conviction and sentence.
Under Army Regulation 190-55, the execution date must fall 60 to 150 days after presidential approval; the Army selected December 3, 2026.
Army planners were still developing firing-squad procedures, including the number of shooters and how Hasan would be secured, because the Army has not used a firing squad since 1945.
Forecast: Hasan could seek a court-ordered delay through further litigation, although AP reported that his conduct at trial may indicate he might not pursue one.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump said Nidal Hasan’s planned execution by firing squad will not be livestreamed, reversing the Pentagon’s earlier public-streaming plan. The execution remains scheduled for Dec. 3, 2026, at Fort Hood, Texas, and immediate family members of victims may attend in person. Trump said a broadcast could have served as a deterrent but also cited the preferences of people who did not want to watch, while the Pentagon has not publicly detailed the viewing arrangements.

sections.heading: Public Broadcast Plan Drew Objections
sections.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had defended public viewing as a way to demonstrate serious consequences for such crimes. But House Speaker Mike Johnson warned that footage could become a recruiting tool for future terrorists. Vice President JD Vance supported the death penalty for Hasan while saying he would not watch a livestream, and Archbishop Paul Coakley called the proposed broadcast a promotion of a culture of death. Officials involved in earlier discussions also worried video could be exploited in extremist propaganda and harm U.S. standing.

sections.heading: Army Set December Execution Schedule
sections.body: The Army said Trump approved Hasan’s death sentence on Oct. 2, 2026, after the appellate process upheld his conviction and sentence. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directed the execution on Oct. 6. Under Army Regulation 190-55, an execution must be scheduled 60 to 150 days after presidential approval; the Army selected Dec. 3. The Army’s Oct. 7 notice set the time at 1 p.m. CST and specified Fort Hood and a firing squad, details Trump’s later statement did not change.

sections.heading: Execution Procedures Remain Undisclosed
sections.body: Army planners were still developing firing-squad procedures, including the number of shooters and how Hasan would be secured, according to reporting on internal deliberations. The Army has not used a firing squad since 1945. Hasan could seek a court-ordered delay through additional litigation, though reporting noted that his conduct at trial may suggest he will not pursue one. As of Oct. 15, no publicly reported filing or court order had established a delay to the Dec. 3 execution.

unresolved.text: The Pentagon has not publicly specified attendance rules or other logistics for in-person viewing by victims’ immediate family members.
The final firing-squad operational protocol, including how Hasan will be secured and the number of shooters, has not been made public.
